title: Small Steps: The Rosenshine Principle That Unlocks the Other Nine
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: The author argues that Rosenshine's principle of presenting new material in small steps with practice after each step is the one that makes the other nine work. The case rests on cognitive science: working memory is small and easily overloaded, so small steps protect it and speed up schema-building. The piece then walks through each of the other principles (review, questioning, modeling, guided and independent practice, scaffolds, high success rate, weekly and monthly review) with a cognitive science tie and a concrete example from a two-day geography lesson comparing food access in the Netherlands and Ethiopia. It closes with a diagnostic for teachers: if questions, retrieval practice, or scaffolds are not working, ask whether too much is being given at once.
points: Small steps reduce cognitive load and protect working memory, which makes them the foundation under Rosenshine's other principles.
Each principle depends on small steps in a specific way: review needs well-encoded material, and questions and checks need a narrow target.
The author's Netherlands and Ethiopia lesson makes the abstract claim concrete by pairing each step with a targeted question, a model, and a short check.
Breaking a broad question into smaller ones gives students visible early success before they attempt synthesis.
A practical diagnostic follows: when other strategies fail, first ask whether the lesson gave too much at once.
quotes: That’s where small steps come in. Breaking new content into bite-sized pieces respects the limits of working memory. It allows students to rehearse, question, and practice each piece before layering on the next.

Over time, these steps link together into strong schemas that free up cognitive space for deeper learning. In short: small steps reduce cognitive load, protect working memory, and accelerate schema-building.

Review is only effective if students actually have something clear and memorable to review. When yesterday’s lesson was taught in small, digestible pieces, today’s review is focused and confidence-building. Without small steps, review turns into vague guessing.
Asking “Any questions?” after a long monologue rarely surfaces confusion. Small steps let you check one idea at a time, making feedback sharper and more actionable.
Scaffolding is often thought of as giving support after the fact, but small steps are scaffolding built in from the start. Each step is itself a scaffold toward the whole.
It’s not the flashiest. But it’s the reason other strategies land. It’s the difference between students feeling overwhelmed and students feeling capable.
If you’re ever wondering why your questions, retrieval practice, or scaffolds don’t seem to be working, start with this check: Am I giving too much at once?
